title: Keys: Super, Candidate, Primary, Foreign
html:
Keys identify rows and link tables. Interviewers love the vocabulary — and the choice between natural and surrogate keys matters in every real schema.

KeyDefinitionIn employees
Super keyAny set of columns that uniquely identifies a row{emp_id}, {email}, {emp_id, name}, …
Candidate keyA minimal super key — remove any column and it is no longer unique{emp_id}, {email} (if always present)
Primary keyThe candidate key chosen as the row's identity; unique and not nullemp_id
Alternate keyA candidate key not chosen as primary (usually enforced with UNIQUE)email
Foreign keyColumn(s) referencing a key of another (or the same) tabledept_id, manager_id
Composite keyA key made of two or more columnsorder_items (order_id, product_id)
Surrogate keyA meaningless generated id (auto-increment, UUID)emp_id
Natural keyA key with business meaningemail, PAN number, ISBN
Super keys
→
minimal → Candidate keys
→
chosen → Primary key
→
others → Alternate keys

Composite primary key

Natural vs surrogate keys

Surrogate (id)

Stable (never changes), compact integer joins, no business meaning to leak. Needs a separate UNIQUE on the natural key to stop duplicates.

Natural (email, ISBN)

Meaningful, no extra column, prevents duplicates by itself. But real-world “unique” values change (emails, phone numbers) or turn out not unique, and wide keys make every foreign key wide.

Do

Common practice: a surrogate primary key plus UNIQUE constraints on the natural candidate keys. Composite natural keys are fine for pure junction tables (order_items).

What is the difference between a primary key and a candidate key?

A candidate key is any minimal set of columns that uniquely identifies rows; a table can have several. The primary key is the one candidate key you choose as the table's official identifier (not null, referenced by foreign keys). The others become alternate keys with UNIQUE constraints.

Can a table have no primary key?

Technically yes in most engines (a heap), but it is almost always a mistake: duplicates can't be prevented or targeted, replication and ORMs struggle, and InnoDB creates a hidden one anyway. Every table should have a primary key.
